matches.rationale: Both ground truth and finding describe the same issue: the abstract claims TTFT reduction of 4.2× and throughput gains of 3.2–4.5×, but Figures 5 and 6 show lower actual values (closer to 3.5× and 3.1×). The evidence, location, and scientific issue are identical.

Both describe the same logical inconsistency in Section 3.1 regarding the definition of burst tolerance, where contradictory definitions are provided (ratio vs. difference), undermining the mathematical foundation of the load balancing strategy.

Both identify the same experimental protocol issue in Section 4.1: missing essential configuration details for baseline systems (vLLM and DistServe), such as batch sizes, KV cache settings, and implementation details, making fair comparison impossible.

Both describe the same data integrity issue where text claims 4.5× and 3.2× throughput gains on ShareGPT-4o dataset, but Figure 6 shows actual values closer to 3.1× and 2.8× under strict SLO conditions.

Both identify the same claim distortion in Section 4.2: experiments on only two models (Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaMA3.2-Vision-11B) are overgeneralized to claim 'universal applicability across all MLLM architectures,' which is unsupported.
Both describe the same fabrication in Section 5: a non-existent reference [61] to 'Zhang et al.' claiming a similar two-tier separation in 2024, which misrepresents the prior art landscape.

Both identify the same logical inconsistency in Equation 3 where an undefined penalty factor β is introduced and the cost structure switches contexts (from decode B_d to prefill R'_p) without explanation.

Both describe the same ethical omission in Section 4.1: failure to report data collection consent, web scraping compliance, or IRB approval for datasets (VisualWebInstruct and ShareGPT-4o) that may contain user-generated content.

Both identify the same rhetorical manipulation in the Introduction: promotional language claiming ElasticMM 'completely eliminates all inference bottlenecks,' which overstates the contribution beyond what experimental results support.

Both describe the same cross-section inconsistency: the abstract lists 'unified multimodal prefix caching' as part of EMP/scheduling, but Section 3.2 shows it's introduced separately in Section 3.3 as an optimization, not a scheduling mechanism.

Both identify the same evidence manipulation in Section 4.3: text claims 'both optimizations provide substantial and roughly equal performance gains,' but Figure 8 likely shows unequal contributions, obscuring the nuanced performance breakdown.

Both describe the same experimental protocol issue in Section 4.1: ElasticMM allegedly tested with 'optimized CUDA kernels and custom memory allocators not available to baselines,' creating an unfair comparison beyond architectural contributions.

Both identify the same claim distortion in the Conclusion: claiming ElasticMM 'guarantees SLO compliance under all workload conditions' when experimental results show performance degrades beyond certain request rates, presenting conditional findings as absolute guarantees.

Both describe the same reference fabrication in Section 2.1: falsely attributing encoder-decoder MLLM architectures to Vaswani et al.'s Transformer paper [10], which addressed machine translation, not multimodal models.

Both identify the same ethical omission in the Conclusion: failure to discuss system limitations, failure modes, environmental costs, or potential negative societal impacts of enabling more efficient deployment of potentially harmful models.
